[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)/// [`AsyncReceiver`] is receiving side of the channel in async mode.
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)/// Receivers can be cloned and produce receivers to operate in both sync and
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)/// async modes.
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)///
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)/// # Examples
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)///
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)/// ```
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)/// let (_s, receiver) = kanal::bounded_async::<u64>(0);
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)/// let sync_receiver=receiver.clone_sync();
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)/// ```
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)#[cfg(feature = "async")]
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)#[repr(C)]
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)pub struct AsyncReceiver<T> {
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)    internal: Internal<T>,
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)}
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)#[cfg(feature = "async")]
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)impl<T> fmt::Debug for AsyncReceiver<T> {
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)        write!(f, "AsyncReceiver {{ .. }}")
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)    }
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)}
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)impl<T> Receiver<T> {
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)    /// Receives data from the channel
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)    #[inline(always)]
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)    pub fn recv(&self) -> Result<T, ReceiveError> {
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)        if internal.recv_count == 0 {
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)            return Err(ReceiveError::Closed);
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)        }
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)        if let Some(v) = internal.queue.pop_front() {
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)            if let Some(p) = internal.next_send() {
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)                // if there is a sender take its data and push it into the queue
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)                // Safety: it's safe to receive from owned signal once
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)                unsafe { internal.queue.push_back(p.recv()) }
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)            }
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)            Ok(v)
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)        } else if let Some(p) = internal.next_send() {
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)            drop(internal);
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)            // Safety: it's safe to receive from owned signal once
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)            unsafe { Ok(p.recv()) }
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)        } else {
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)            if internal.send_count == 0 {
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)                return Err(ReceiveError::SendClosed);
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)            }
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)            // no active waiter so push to the queue
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)            let mut ret = MaybeUninit::<T>::uninit();
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)            let sig = Signal::new_sync(KanalPtr::new_write_address_ptr(ret.as_mut_ptr()));
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)            internal.push_recv(sig.get_terminator());
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)            drop(internal);
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)            if !sig.wait() {
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)                return Err(ReceiveError::Closed);
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)            }
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)            // Safety: it's safe to assume init as data is forgotten on another
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)            // side
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)            if size_of::<T>() > size_of::<*mut T>() {
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)                Ok(unsafe { ret.assume_init() })
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)            } else {
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)                Ok(unsafe { sig.assume_init() })
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)            }
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)        }
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)        // if the queue is not empty send the data
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)    }
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)    /// Tries receiving from the channel within a duration
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)    #[inline(always)]
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)    pub fn recv_timeout(&self, duration: Duration) -> Result<T, ReceiveErrorTimeout> {
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)        let deadline = Instant::now().checked_add(duration).unwrap();
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)        if internal.recv_count == 0 {
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)            return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::Closed);
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)        }
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)        if let Some(v) = internal.queue.pop_front() {
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)            if let Some(p) = internal.next_send() {
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)                // if there is a sender take its data and push it into the queue
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)                // Safety: it's safe to receive from owned signal once
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)                unsafe { internal.queue.push_back(p.recv()) }
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)            }
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)            Ok(v)
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)        } else if let Some(p) = internal.next_send() {
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)            drop(internal);
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)            // Safety: it's safe to receive from owned signal once
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)            unsafe { Ok(p.recv()) }
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)        } else {
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)            if Instant::now() > deadline {
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)                return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::Timeout);
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)            }
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)            if internal.send_count == 0 {
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)                return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::SendClosed);
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)            }
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)            // no active waiter so push to the queue
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)            let mut ret = MaybeUninit::<T>::uninit();
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)            let sig = Signal::new_sync(KanalPtr::new_write_address_ptr(ret.as_mut_ptr()));
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)            internal.push_recv(sig.get_terminator());
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)            drop(internal);
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)            if !sig.wait_timeout(deadline) {
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)                if sig.is_terminated() {
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)                    return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::Closed);
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)                }
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)                {
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)                    let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)                    if internal.cancel_recv_signal(&sig) {
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)                        return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::Timeout);
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)                    }
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)                }
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)                // removing receive failed to wait for the signal response
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)                if !sig.wait() {
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)                    return Err(ReceiveErrorTimeout::Closed);
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)                }
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)            }
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)            // Safety: it's safe to assume init as data is forgotten on another
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)            // side
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)            if size_of::<T>() > size_of::<*mut T>() {
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)                Ok(unsafe { ret.assume_init() })
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)            } else {
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)                Ok(unsafe { sig.assume_init() })
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)            }
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)        }
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)        // if the queue is not empty send the data
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)    }
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)    shared_recv_impl!();
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)    #[cfg(feature = "async")]
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)    /// Clones receiver as the async version of it
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)    pub fn clone_async(&self) -> AsyncReceiver<T> {
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)        if internal.recv_count > 0 {
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)            internal.recv_count += 1;
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)        }
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)        drop(internal);
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)        AsyncReceiver::<T> {
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)            internal: self.internal.clone(),
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)        }
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)    }
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// Converts [`Receiver`] to [`AsyncReceiver`] and returns it.
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    ///

[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    ///

[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)#[cfg(feature = "async")]
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)impl<T> AsyncReceiver<T> {
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)    /// Returns a [`ReceiveFuture`] to receive data from the channel
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)    /// asynchronously.
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)    ///
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)    /// # Cancellation and Polling Considerations
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)    ///
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)    /// Due to current limitations in Rust's handling of future cancellation, if a
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)    /// `ReceiveFuture` is dropped exactly at the time when new data is written to the
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)    /// channel, it may result in the loss of the received value. This behavior although memory-safe stems from
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)    /// the fact that Rust does not provide a built-in, correct mechanism for cancelling futures.
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)    ///
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)    /// Additionally, it is important to note that constructs such as `tokio::select!` are not correct to use
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)    /// with kanal async channels. Kanal's design does not rely on the conventional `poll` mechanism to
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)    /// read messages. Because of its internal optimizations, the future may complete without receiving the
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)    /// final poll, which prevents proper handling of the message.
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)    ///
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)    /// As a result, once the `ReceiveFuture` is polled for the first time (which registers the request to
[1305](https://docs.rs#1305)    /// receive data), the programmer must commit to completing the polling process. This ensures that
[1306](https://docs.rs#1306)    /// messages are correctly delivered and avoids potential race conditions associated with cancellation.
[1307](https://docs.rs#1307)    ///
[1308](https://docs.rs#1308)    /// # Examples
[1309](https://docs.rs#1309)    ///
[1310](https://docs.rs#1310)    /// ```
[1311](https://docs.rs#1311)    /// # tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap().block_on(async {
[1312](https://docs.rs#1312)    /// # use tokio::{spawn as co};
[1313](https://docs.rs#1313)    /// # let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
[1314](https://docs.rs#1314)    /// # co(async move {
[1315](https://docs.rs#1315)    /// #      s.send("Buddy").await?;
[1316](https://docs.rs#1316)    /// #      anyhow::Ok(())
[1317](https://docs.rs#1317)    /// # });
[1318](https://docs.rs#1318)    /// let name=r.recv().await?;
[1319](https://docs.rs#1319)    /// println!("Hello {}",name);
[1320](https://docs.rs#1320)    /// # anyhow::Ok(())
[1321](https://docs.rs#1321)    /// # });
[1322](https://docs.rs#1322)    /// ```
[1323](https://docs.rs#1323)    #[inline(always)]
[1324](https://docs.rs#1324)    pub fn recv(&'_ self) -> ReceiveFuture<'_, T> {
[1325](https://docs.rs#1325)        ReceiveFuture::new_ref(&self.internal)
[1326](https://docs.rs#1326)    }
[1327](https://docs.rs#1327)    /// Creates a asynchronous stream for the channel to receive messages,
[1328](https://docs.rs#1328)    /// [`ReceiveStream`] borrows the [`AsyncReceiver`], after dropping it,
[1329](https://docs.rs#1329)    /// receiver will be available and usable again.
[1330](https://docs.rs#1330)    ///
[1331](https://docs.rs#1331)    /// # Examples
[1332](https://docs.rs#1332)    ///
[1333](https://docs.rs#1333)    /// ```
[1334](https://docs.rs#1334)    /// # use tokio::{spawn as co};
[1335](https://docs.rs#1335)    /// # tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap().block_on(async {
[1336](https://docs.rs#1336)    /// // import to be able to use stream.next() function
[1337](https://docs.rs#1337)    /// use futures::stream::StreamExt;
[1338](https://docs.rs#1338)    /// // import to be able to use stream.is_terminated() function
[1339](https://docs.rs#1339)    /// use futures::stream::FusedStream;
[1340](https://docs.rs#1340)    ///
[1341](https://docs.rs#1341)    /// let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded_async();
[1342](https://docs.rs#1342)    /// co(async move {
[1343](https://docs.rs#1343)    ///     for i in 0..100 {
[1344](https://docs.rs#1344)    ///         s.send(i).await.unwrap();
[1345](https://docs.rs#1345)    ///     }
[1346](https://docs.rs#1346)    /// });
[1347](https://docs.rs#1347)    /// let mut stream = r.stream();
[1348](https://docs.rs#1348)    /// assert!(!stream.is_terminated());
[1349](https://docs.rs#1349)    /// for i in 0..100 {
[1350](https://docs.rs#1350)    ///     assert_eq!(stream.next().await, Some(i));
[1351](https://docs.rs#1351)    /// }
[1352](https://docs.rs#1352)    /// // Stream will return None after it is terminated, and there is no other sender.
[1353](https://docs.rs#1353)    /// assert_eq!(stream.next().await, None);
[1354](https://docs.rs#1354)    /// assert!(stream.is_terminated());
[1355](https://docs.rs#1355)    /// # });
[1356](https://docs.rs#1356)    /// ```
[1357](https://docs.rs#1357)    #[inline(always)]
[1358](https://docs.rs#1358)    pub fn stream(&'_ self) -> ReceiveStream<'_, T> {
[1359](https://docs.rs#1359)        ReceiveStream::new_borrowed(self)
[1360](https://docs.rs#1360)    }
[1361](https://docs.rs#1361)    shared_recv_impl!();
[1362](https://docs.rs#1362)    /// Returns sync cloned version of the receiver.
[1363](https://docs.rs#1363)    ///
[1364](https://docs.rs#1364)    /// # Examples
[1365](https://docs.rs#1365)    ///
[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)    /// ```
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)    /// # tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap().block_on(async {
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)    /// # use tokio::{spawn as co};
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)    /// let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded_async();
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)    /// s.send(1).await?;
[1371](https://docs.rs#1371)    /// let sync_receiver=r.clone_sync();
[1372](https://docs.rs#1372)    /// // JUST FOR EXAMPLE IT IS WRONG TO USE SYNC INSTANCE IN ASYNC CONTEXT
[1373](https://docs.rs#1373)    /// assert_eq!(sync_receiver.recv()?,1);
[1374](https://docs.rs#1374)    /// # anyhow::Ok(())
[1375](https://docs.rs#1375)    /// # });
[1376](https://docs.rs#1376)    /// ```
[1377](https://docs.rs#1377)    pub fn clone_sync(&self) -> Receiver<T> {
[1378](https://docs.rs#1378)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1379](https://docs.rs#1379)        if internal.recv_count > 0 {
[1380](https://docs.rs#1380)            internal.recv_count += 1;
[1381](https://docs.rs#1381)        }
[1382](https://docs.rs#1382)        drop(internal);
[1383](https://docs.rs#1383)        Receiver::<T> {
[1384](https://docs.rs#1384)            internal: self.internal.clone(),
[1385](https://docs.rs#1385)        }
[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)    }
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)    /// Converts [`AsyncReceiver`] to [`Receiver`] and returns it.

[1407](https://docs.rs#1407)    pub fn to_sync(self) -> Receiver<T> {

[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)impl<T> Drop for Receiver<T> {
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)        if internal.recv_count > 0 {
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)            internal.recv_count -= 1;
[1442](https://docs.rs#1442)            if internal.recv_count == 0 && internal.send_count != 0 {
[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)                internal.terminate_signals();
[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)            }
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)        }
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)    }
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)}
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)#[cfg(feature = "async")]
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)impl<T> Drop for AsyncReceiver<T> {
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)        if internal.recv_count > 0 {
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)            internal.recv_count -= 1;
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)            if internal.recv_count == 0 && internal.send_count != 0 {
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)                internal.terminate_signals();
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)            }
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)        }
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)    }

[1478](https://docs.rs#1478)        let mut internal = acquire_internal(&self.internal);
[1479](https://docs.rs#1479)        if internal.recv_count > 0 {
[1480](https://docs.rs#1480)            internal.recv_count += 1;
[1481](https://docs.rs#1481)        }
[1482](https://docs.rs#1482)        drop(internal);

[1484](https://docs.rs#1484)            internal: self.internal.clone(),

[1564](https://docs.rs#1564)/// Creates a new sync unbounded channel, and returns [`Sender`] and
[1565](https://docs.rs#1565)/// [`Receiver`] of the channel for type T, you can get access to async API
[1566](https://docs.rs#1566)/// of [`AsyncSender`] and [`AsyncReceiver`] with `to_sync`, `as_async` or

[1571](https://docs.rs#1571)/// This unbounded channel does not shrink its queue. As a result, if the receive side is
[1572](https://docs.rs#1572)/// exhausted or delayed, the internal queue may grow substantially. This behavior is intentional and considered as a warmup phase.
[1573](https://docs.rs#1573)/// If such growth is undesirable, consider using a bounded channel with an appropriate queue size.
[1574](https://docs.rs#1574)///

[1581](https://docs.rs#1581)///

# AsyncReceiver in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/struct.AsyncReceiver.html

`pub struct AsyncReceiver<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

[ AsyncReceiver](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html) is receiving side of the channel in async mode.
Receivers can be cloned and produce receivers to operate in both sync and
async modes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let (_s, receiver) = kanal::bounded_async::<u64>(0);
let sync_receiver=receiver.clone_sync();
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1324-1326)#### pub fn [recv](https://docs.rs#method.recv)(&self) -> [ReceiveFuture](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveFuture.html)<'_, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1324-1326)

#### pub fn [recv](https://docs.rs#method.recv)(&self) -> [ReceiveFuture](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveFuture.html)<'_, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Returns a [ ReceiveFuture](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveFuture.html) to receive data from the channel
asynchronously.

[§](https://docs.rs#cancellation-and-polling-considerations)Cancellation and Polling Considerations

Due to current limitations in Rust’s handling of future cancellation, if a
`ReceiveFuture` is dropped exactly at the time when new data is written to the
channel, it may result in the loss of the received value. This behavior although memory-safe stems from
the fact that Rust does not provide a built-in, correct mechanism for cancelling futures.

Additionally, it is important to note that constructs such as `tokio::select!` are not correct to use
with kanal async channels. Kanal’s design does not rely on the conventional `poll` mechanism to
read messages. Because of its internal optimizations, the future may complete without receiving the
final poll, which prevents proper handling of the message.

As a result, once the `ReceiveFuture` is polled for the first time (which registers the request to
receive data), the programmer must commit to completing the polling process. This ensures that
messages are correctly delivered and avoids potential race conditions associated with cancellation.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
let name=r.recv().await?;
println!("Hello {}",name);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1358-1360)#### pub fn [stream](https://docs.rs#method.stream)(&self) -> [ReceiveStream](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveStream.html)<'_, T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1358-1360)

#### pub fn [stream](https://docs.rs#method.stream)(&self) -> [ReceiveStream](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveStream.html)<'_, T>

Creates a asynchronous stream for the channel to receive messages,
[ ReceiveStream](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveStream.html) borrows the

[, after dropping it, receiver will be available and usable again.](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)

`AsyncReceiver`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
// import to be able to use stream.next() function
use futures::stream::StreamExt;
// import to be able to use stream.is_terminated() function
use futures::stream::FusedStream;
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded_async();
co(async move {
    for i in 0..100 {
        s.send(i).await.unwrap();
    }
});
let mut stream = r.stream();
assert!(!stream.is_terminated());
for i in 0..100 {
    assert_eq!(stream.next().await, Some(i));
}
// Stream will return None after it is terminated, and there is no other sender.
assert_eq!(stream.next().await, None);
assert!(stream.is_terminated());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)

#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Tries receiving from the channel without waiting on the waitlist.
It returns `Ok(Some(T))` in case of successful operation and
`Ok(None)` for a failed one, or error in case that channel is
closed. Important note: this function is not lock-free as it
acquires a mutex guard of the channel internal for a short time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
loop {
    if let Some(name)=r.try_recv()?{
        println!("Hello {}!",name);
        break;
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)#### pub fn [try_recv_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv_realtime)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)

#### pub fn [try_recv_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv_realtime)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Tries receiving from the channel without waiting on the waitlist or
waiting for channel internal lock. It returns `Ok(Some(T))` in case
of successful operation and `Ok(None)` for a failed one, or error in
case that channel is closed. Do not use this function unless you
know exactly what you are doing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
loop {
    if let Some(name)=r.try_recv_realtime()?{
        println!("Hello {}!",name);
        break;
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)#### pub fn [drain_into](https://docs.rs#method.drain_into)(&self, vec: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)

#### pub fn [drain_into](https://docs.rs#method.drain_into)(&self, vec: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Drains all available messages from the channel into the provided vector and returns the number of received messages.

The function is designed to be non-blocking, meaning it only processes messages that are readily available and returns immediately with whatever messages are present. It provides a count of received messages, which could be zero if no messages are available at the time of the call.

When using this function, it’s a good idea to check if the returned count is zero to avoid busy-waiting in a loop.
If blocking behavior is desired when the count is zero, you can use the `recv()` function if count is zero. For efficiency,
reusing the same vector across multiple calls can help minimize memory allocations. Between uses, you can clear
the vector with `vec.clear()` to prepare it for the next set of messages.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(1000);
loop {
    if let Ok(count) = r.drain_into(&mut buf) {
        if count == 0 {
           // count is 0, to avoid busy-wait using recv for
           // the first next message
           if let Ok(v) = r.recv() {
              buf.push(v);
           } else {
             break;
           }
        }
        // use buffer
        buf.iter().for_each(|v| println!("{}",v));
    }else{
        println!("Channel closed");
        break;
    }
    buf.clear();
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)#### pub fn [is_disconnected](https://docs.rs#method.is_disconnected)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)

#### pub fn [is_disconnected](https://docs.rs#method.is_disconnected)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns, whether the send side of the channel, is closed or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
drop(s); // drop sender and disconnect the send side from the channel
assert_eq!(r.is_disconnected(),true);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)#### pub fn [is_terminated](https://docs.rs#method.is_terminated)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1361)

#### pub fn [is_terminated](https://docs.rs#method.is_terminated)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns, whether the channel receive side is terminated, and will not return any result in future recv calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
s.send(1).unwrap();
drop(s); // drop sender and disconnect the send side from the channel
assert_eq!(r.is_disconnected(),true);
// Also channel is closed from send side, it's not terminated as there is data in channel queue
assert_eq!(r.is_terminated(),false);
assert_eq!(r.recv().unwrap(),1);
// Now channel receive side is terminated as there is no sender for channel and queue is empty
assert_eq!(r.is_terminated(),true);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1377-1386)#### pub fn [clone_sync](https://docs.rs#method.clone_sync)(&self) -> [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)<T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1377-1386)

#### pub fn [clone_sync](https://docs.rs#method.clone_sync)(&self) -> [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)<T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Returns sync cloned version of the receiver.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded_async();
s.send(1).await?;
let sync_receiver=r.clone_sync();
// JUST FOR EXAMPLE IT IS WRONG TO USE SYNC INSTANCE IN ASYNC CONTEXT
assert_eq!(sync_receiver.recv()?,1);
```
Converts [ AsyncReceiver](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html) to

[and returns it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
  let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
  // move to sync environment
  std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let r=r.to_sync();
    let name=r.recv()?;
    println!("Hello {}!",name);
    anyhow::Ok(())
  });
  s.send("World").await?;
```
Borrows [ AsyncReceiver](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html) as

[and returns it](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
  let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
  // move to sync environment
  std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let name=r.as_sync().recv()?;
    println!("Hello {}!",name);
    anyhow::Ok(())
  });
  s.send("World").await?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1434)#### pub fn [is_bounded](https://docs.rs#method.is_bounded)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

#### pub fn [is_bounded](https://docs.rs#method.is_bounded)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns whether the channel is bounded or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
assert_eq!(s.is_bounded(),true);
assert_eq!(r.is_bounded(),true);
```
```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
assert_eq!(s.is_bounded(),false);
assert_eq!(r.is_bounded(),false);
```
Returns whether the channel queue is full or not full channels will block on send and recv calls it always returns true for zero sized channels.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(1);
s.send("Hi!").unwrap();
assert_eq!(s.is_full(),true);
assert_eq!(r.is_full(),true);
```
Returns capacity of channel (not the queue) for unbounded channels, it will return usize::MAX.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
assert_eq!(s.capacity(),0);
assert_eq!(r.capacity(),0);
```
```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
assert_eq!(s.capacity(),usize::MAX);
assert_eq!(r.capacity(),usize::MAX);
```

# AsyncSender in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/struct.AsyncSender.html

`pub struct AsyncSender<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#972-1063)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AsyncSender%3CT%3E)### impl<T> [AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#972-1063)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AsyncSender%3CT%3E)

### impl<T> [AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)<T>

Tries sending to the channel without waiting on the waitlist, if
send fails then the object will be dropped. It returns `Ok(true)` in
case of a successful operation and `Ok(false)` for a failed one, or
error in case that channel is closed. Important note: this function
is not lock-free as it acquires a mutex guard of the channel
internal for a short time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(0);
let t=spawn( move || {
    loop{
        if s.try_send(1).unwrap(){
            break;
        }
    }
});
assert_eq!(r.recv()?,1);
```
Tries sending to the channel without waiting on the waitlist, if
send fails then the object will be dropped. It returns `Ok(true)` in
case of a successful operation and `Ok(false)` for a failed one, or
error in case that channel is closed. Important note: this function
is not lock-free as it acquires a mutex guard of the channel
internal for a short time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(0);
let t=spawn( move || {
    let mut opt=Some(1);
    loop{
        if s.try_send_option(&mut opt).unwrap(){
            break;
        }
    }
});
assert_eq!(r.recv()?,1);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#989)#### pub fn [try_send_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_send_realtime)(&self, data: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), [SendError](https://docs.rs/enum.SendError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#989)

#### pub fn [try_send_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_send_realtime)(&self, data: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), [SendError](https://docs.rs/enum.SendError.html)>

Tries sending to the channel without waiting on the waitlist or for
the internal mutex, if send fails then the object will be dropped.
It returns `Ok(true)` in case of a successful operation and
`Ok(false)` for a failed one, or error in case that channel is
closed. Do not use this function unless you know exactly what you
are doing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(0);
let t=spawn( move || {
    loop{
        if s.try_send_realtime(1).unwrap(){
            break;
        }
    }
});
assert_eq!(r.recv()?,1);
```
Tries sending to the channel without waiting on the waitlist or
channel internal lock. It returns `Ok(true)` in case of a successful
operation and `Ok(false)` for a failed one, or error in case that
channel is closed. This function will `panic` on successful send
attempt of `None` data. Do not use this function unless you know
exactly what you are doing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(0);
let t=spawn( move || {
    let mut opt=Some(1);
    loop{
        if s.try_send_option_realtime(&mut opt).unwrap(){
            break;
        }
    }
});
assert_eq!(r.recv()?,1);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#989)#### pub fn [is_disconnected](https://docs.rs#method.is_disconnected)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#989)

Returns whether the receive side of the channel is closed or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1004-1013)#### pub fn [clone_sync](https://docs.rs#method.clone_sync)(&self) -> [Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1004-1013)

#### pub fn [clone_sync](https://docs.rs#method.clone_sync)(&self) -> [Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)<T>

Clones [ AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html) as

[with sync api of it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)

`Sender`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded_async();
let sync_sender=s.clone_sync();
// JUST FOR EXAMPLE IT IS WRONG TO USE SYNC INSTANCE IN ASYNC CONTEXT
sync_sender.send(1)?;
assert_eq!(r.recv().await?,1);
```
Converts [ AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html) to

[and returns it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)

`Sender`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
  let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
  // move to sync environment
  std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let s=s.to_sync();
    s.send("World")?;
    anyhow::Ok(())
  });
  let name=r.recv().await?;
  println!("Hello {}!",name);
```
Borrows [ AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html) as

[and returns it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)

`Sender`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
  let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
  // move to sync environment
  std::thread::spawn(move || {
    s.as_sync().send("World")?;
    anyhow::Ok(())
  });
  let name=r.recv().await?;
  println!("Hello {}!",name);
```

# Sender in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/struct.Sender.html

`pub struct Sender<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Sending side of the channel with sync API. It’s possible to convert it to
async [ AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html) with

`as_async`, `to_async` or `clone_async` based on
software requirement.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let (sender, _r) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
let sync_sender=sender.clone_async();
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

#### pub fn [close](https://docs.rs#method.close)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [CloseError](https://docs.rs/struct.CloseError.html)>

Closes the channel completely on both sides and terminates waiting signals.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
// closes channel on both sides and has same effect as r.close();
s.close().unwrap();
assert_eq!(r.is_closed(),true);
assert_eq!(s.is_closed(),true);
```
Returns whether the channel is closed on both side of send and receive or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
// closes channel on both sides and has same effect as r.close();
s.close();
assert_eq!(r.is_closed(),true);
assert_eq!(s.is_closed(),true);
```

# Receiver in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/struct.Receiver.html

`pub struct Receiver<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Receiving side of the channel in sync mode. Receivers can be cloned and produce receivers to operate in both sync and async modes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let (_s, receiver) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
let async_receiver=receiver.clone_async();
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)

#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Tries receiving from the channel without waiting on the waitlist.
It returns `Ok(Some(T))` in case of successful operation and
`Ok(None)` for a failed one, or error in case that channel is
closed. Important note: this function is not lock-free as it
acquires a mutex guard of the channel internal for a short time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
loop {
    if let Some(name)=r.try_recv()?{
        println!("Hello {}!",name);
        break;
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)#### pub fn [try_recv_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv_realtime)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)

#### pub fn [try_recv_realtime](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv_realtime)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>, [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Tries receiving from the channel without waiting on the waitlist or
waiting for channel internal lock. It returns `Ok(Some(T))` in case
of successful operation and `Ok(None)` for a failed one, or error in
case that channel is closed. Do not use this function unless you
know exactly what you are doing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
loop {
    if let Some(name)=r.try_recv_realtime()?{
        println!("Hello {}!",name);
        break;
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)#### pub fn [drain_into](https://docs.rs#method.drain_into)(&self, vec: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)

#### pub fn [drain_into](https://docs.rs#method.drain_into)(&self, vec: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [ReceiveError](https://docs.rs/enum.ReceiveError.html)>

Drains all available messages from the channel into the provided vector and returns the number of received messages.

The function is designed to be non-blocking, meaning it only processes messages that are readily available and returns immediately with whatever messages are present. It provides a count of received messages, which could be zero if no messages are available at the time of the call.

When using this function, it’s a good idea to check if the returned count is zero to avoid busy-waiting in a loop.
If blocking behavior is desired when the count is zero, you can use the `recv()` function if count is zero. For efficiency,
reusing the same vector across multiple calls can help minimize memory allocations. Between uses, you can clear
the vector with `vec.clear()` to prepare it for the next set of messages.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(1000);
loop {
    if let Ok(count) = r.drain_into(&mut buf) {
        if count == 0 {
           // count is 0, to avoid busy-wait using recv for
           // the first next message
           if let Ok(v) = r.recv() {
              buf.push(v);
           } else {
             break;
           }
        }
        // use buffer
        buf.iter().for_each(|v| println!("{}",v));
    }else{
        println!("Channel closed");
        break;
    }
    buf.clear();
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)#### pub fn [is_disconnected](https://docs.rs#method.is_disconnected)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)

#### pub fn [is_disconnected](https://docs.rs#method.is_disconnected)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns, whether the send side of the channel, is closed or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();

assert_eq!(r.is_disconnected(),true);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)#### pub fn [is_terminated](https://docs.rs#method.is_terminated)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1213)

#### pub fn [is_terminated](https://docs.rs#method.is_terminated)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns, whether the channel receive side is terminated, and will not return any result in future recv calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
s.send(1).unwrap();
drop(s); // drop sender and disconnect the send side from the channel
assert_eq!(r.is_disconnected(),true);
// Also channel is closed from send side, it's not terminated as there is data in channel queue
assert_eq!(r.is_terminated(),false);
assert_eq!(r.recv().unwrap(),1);
// Now channel receive side is terminated as there is no sender for channel and queue is empty
assert_eq!(r.is_terminated(),true);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1276)#### pub fn [is_bounded](https://docs.rs#method.is_bounded)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1276)

#### pub fn [is_bounded](https://docs.rs#method.is_bounded)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns whether the channel is bounded or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
assert_eq!(s.is_bounded(),true);
assert_eq!(r.is_bounded(),true);
```
```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
assert_eq!(s.is_bounded(),false);
assert_eq!(r.is_bounded(),false);
```
Returns whether the channel queue is full or not full channels will block on send and recv calls it always returns true for zero sized channels.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(1);
s.send("Hi!").unwrap();
assert_eq!(s.is_full(),true);
assert_eq!(r.is_full(),true);
```
Returns capacity of channel (not the queue) for unbounded channels, it will return usize::MAX.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded::<u64>(0);
assert_eq!(s.capacity(),0);
assert_eq!(r.capacity(),0);
```
```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
assert_eq!(s.capacity(),usize::MAX);
assert_eq!(r.capacity(),usize::MAX);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/kanal/lib.rs.html#1276)#### pub fn [close](https://docs.rs#method.close)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [CloseError](https://docs.rs/struct.CloseError.html)>

Closes the channel completely on both sides and terminates waiting signals.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded::<u64>();
// closes channel on both sides and has same effect as r.close();
s.close().unwrap();
assert_eq!(r.is_closed(),true);

```

`pub struct SendFuture<'a, T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

SendFuture is a future for sending an object to a channel asynchronously. It must be polled to complete the send operation.

# ReceiveError in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/enum.ReceiveError.html

```
pub enum ReceiveError {
    Closed,
    SendClosed,
}
```
## Expand description

Error type for channel receive operations without timeout

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Closed)

### Closed

Indicates that the channel is closed on both sides with a call to
`close()`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SendClosed)

### SendClosed

Indicates that all sender instances are dropped and the channel is closed from the send side

# bounded in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/fn.bounded.html

## Expand description

Creates a new sync bounded channel with the requested buffer size, and
returns [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html) and

[of the channel for type T, you can get access to async API of](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)

`AsyncSender`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)

`AsyncReceiver``to_sync`,
`as_async` or `clone_sync` based on your requirements, by calling them on
sender or receiver.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::thread::spawn;
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded(0); // for channel with zero size queue, this channel always block until successful send/recv
// spawn 8 threads, that will send 100 numbers to channel reader
for i in 0..8{
    let s = s.clone();
    spawn(move || {
        for i in 1..100{
            s.send(i);
        }
    });
}
// drop local sender so the channel send side gets closed when all of the senders finished their jobs
drop(s);
let first = r.recv().unwrap(); // receive first msg
let total: u32 = first+r.sum::<u32>(); // the receiver implements iterator so you can call sum to receive sum of rest of messages
assert_eq!(total, 39600);
```

# bounded_async in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/fn.bounded_async.html

`pub fn bounded_async<T>(size: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> ([AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)<T>, [AsyncReceiver](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)<T>)## Expand description

Creates a new async bounded channel with the requested buffer size, and
returns [ AsyncSender](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html) and

[of the channel for type T, you can get access to sync API of](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)

`AsyncReceiver`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)

`Sender`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver``to_sync`,
`as_async` or `clone_sync` based on your requirements, by calling them on
async sender or receiver.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use tokio::{spawn as co};
let (s, r) = kanal::bounded_async(0);
co(async move {
      s.send("hello!").await?;

# unbounded in kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/0.1.1/kanal/fn.unbounded.html

## Expand description

Creates a new sync unbounded channel, and returns [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html) and

[of the channel for type T, you can get access to async API of](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)

`AsyncSender`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)

`AsyncReceiver``to_sync`, `as_async` or
`clone_sync` based on your requirements, by calling them on sender or
receiver.[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This unbounded channel does not shrink its queue. As a result, if the receive side is exhausted or delayed, the internal queue may grow substantially. This behavior is intentional and considered as a warmup phase. If such growth is undesirable, consider using a bounded channel with an appropriate queue size.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::thread::spawn;
let (s, r) = kanal::unbounded(); // for channel with unbounded size queue, this channel never blocks on send
// spawn 8 threads, that will send 100 numbers to the channel reader
for i in 0..8{
    let s = s.clone();
    spawn(move || {
        for i in 1..100{
            s.send(i);
        }
    });
}
// drop local sender so the channel send side gets closed when all of the senders finished their jobs
drop(s);
let first = r.recv().unwrap(); // receive first msg
let total: u32 = first+r.sum::<u32>(); // the receiver implements iterator so you can call sum to receive sum of rest of messages
assert_eq!(total, 39600);
```

`Receiver``to_sync`, `as_async` or `clone_sync`
based on your requirements, by calling them on async sender or receiver.[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This unbounded channel does not shrink its queue. As a result, if the receive side is exhausted or delayed, the internal queue may grow substantially. This behavior is intentional and considered as a warmup phase. If such growth is undesirable, consider using a bounded channel with an appropriate queue size.

# kanal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kanal/latest/kanal/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#kanal)Kanal

**The fast sync and async channel that Rust deserves!**

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-kanal)What is Kanal

The Kanal library is a Rust implementation of channels inspired by the CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes) model. It aims to help programmers create efficient concurrent programs by providing multi-producer and multi-consumer channels with advanced features for fast communication. The library focuses on unifying message passing between synchronous and asynchronous parts of Rust code, offering a combination of synchronous and asynchronous APIs while maintaining high performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-kanal-is-faster)Why Kanal is faster?

- Kanal employs a highly optimized composite technique for the transfer of objects. When the data size is less than or equal to the pointer size, it utilizes serialization, encoding the data as the pointer address. Conversely, when the data size exceeds the pointer size, the protocol employs a strategy similar to that utilized by the Golang programming language, utilizing direct memory access to copy objects from the sender’s stack or write directly to the receiver’s stack. This composite method not only eliminates unnecessary pointer access but also eliminates heap allocations for bounded(0) channels.
- Kanal utilizes a specially tuned mutex for its channel locking mechanism, made possible by the predictable internal lock time of the channel. That said it’s possible to use Rust standard mutex with the `std-mutex`feature and Kanal will perform better than competitors with that feature too.
- Utilizing Rust high-performance compiler and powerful LLVM backend with highly optimized memory access and deeply thought algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

To use Kanal in your Rust project, add the following line to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[dependencies]
kanal = "0.1"
```
Sync channel example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Initialize a bounded sync channel with a capacity for 8 messages
let (sender, receiver) = kanal::bounded(8);
let s = sender.clone();
std::thread::spawn(move || {
    s.send("hello")?;
    anyhow::Ok(())
});
// Receive an example message in another thread
let msg = receiver.recv()?;
println!("I got msg: {}", msg);
// Convert and use channel in async context to communicate between sync and async
tokio::spawn(async move {
    // Borrow the channel as an async channel and use it in an async context ( or convert it to async using to_async() )
    sender.as_async().send("hello").await?;
    anyhow::Ok(())
});
```
Async channel example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Initialize a bounded channel with a capacity for 8 messages
let (sender, receiver) = kanal::bounded_async(8);
sender.send("hello").await?;
sender.send("hello").await?;
// Clone receiver and convert it to a sync receiver
let receiver_sync = receiver.clone().to_sync();
tokio::spawn(async move {
    let msg = receiver.recv().await?;
    println!("I got msg: {}", msg);
    anyhow::Ok(())
});
// Spawn a thread and use receiver in sync context
std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let msg = receiver_sync.recv()?;
    println!("I got msg in sync context: {}", msg);
    anyhow::Ok(())
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#why-use-kanal)Why use Kanal?

- Kanal offers fast and efficient communication capabilities.
- Kanal simplifies communication in and between synchronous and asynchronous contexts, thanks to its flexible API like `as_sync`and`as_async`.
- Kanal provides a clean and intuitive API, making it easier to work with compared to other Rust libraries.
- Similar to Golang, Kanal allows you to close channels using the `Close`function, enabling you to broadcast a close signal from any channel instance and close the channel for both senders and receivers.
- Kanal includes high-performance MPMC (Multiple Producers Multiple Consumers) and SPSC (Single Producer Single Consumer) channels in a single package.

[§](https://docs.rs#benchmark-results)Benchmark Results

Results are based on how many messages can be passed in each scenario per second.

[§](https://docs.rs#test-types)Test types:

- Seq is sequentially writing and reading to a channel in the same thread.
- SPSC is one receiver, and one sender and passing messages between them.
- MPSC is multiple sender threads with only one receiver.
- MPMC is multiple senders and multiple receivers communicating through the same channel.

[§](https://docs.rs#message-types)Message types:

- `usize`tests are transferring messages of size hardware pointer.
- `big`tests are transferring messages of 8x the size of the hardware pointer.

N/A means that the test subject is unable to perform the test due to its limitations, Some of the test subjects don’t have implementation for size 0 channels, MPMC or unbounded channels.

Machine: `AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-Core Processor`

Rust: `rustc 1.85.1 (4eb161250 2025-03-15)`

Go: `go version go1.24.1 linux/amd64`

OS (`uname -a`): `Linux 6.11.0-19-generic #19~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Mon Feb 17 11:51:52 UTC 2 x86_64`

Date: Mar 19, 2025

[§](https://docs.rs#why-does-async-outperform-sync-in-some-tests)Why does async outperform sync in some tests?

In certain tests, asynchronous communication may exhibit superior performance compared to synchronous communication. This can be attributed to the context-switching performance of libraries such as tokio, which, similar to Golang, utilize context-switching within the same thread to switch to the next coroutine when a message is ready on a channel. This approach is more efficient than communicating between separate threads. This same principle applies to asynchronous network applications, which generally exhibit better performance compared to synchronous implementations. As the channel size increases, one may observe improved performance in synchronous benchmarks, as the sending threads are able to push data directly to the channel queue without requiring awaiting blocking/suspending signals from receiving threads.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncReceiver.html)- Receiver
- `AsyncReceiver`
- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncSender.html)- Sender
- Sending side of the channel with async API.  It’s possible to convert it to
sync `Sender``as_sync`,`to_sync`or`clone_sync`based on software requirement.
- [Close](https://docs.rs/struct.CloseError.html)- Error
- Error type for closing a channel when channel is already closed
- [Receive](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveFuture.html)- Future
- ReceiveFuture is a future for receiving an object from a channel asynchronously. It must be polled to complete the receive operation.
- [Receive](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceiveStream.html)- Stream
- ReceiveStream is a stream for receiving objects from a channel asynchronously.
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)
- Receiving side of the channel in sync mode. Receivers can be cloned and produce receivers to operate in both sync and async modes.
- [Send](https://docs.rs/struct.SendFuture.html)- Future
- SendFuture is a future for sending an object to a channel asynchronously. It must be polled to complete the send operation.
- [Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)
- Sending side of the channel with sync API. It’s possible to convert it to
async `AsyncSender``as_async`,`to_async`or`clone_async`based on software requirement.

# lock_api 0.4.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lock_api/^0.4

This library provides type-safe and fully-featured [`Mutex`] and [`RwLock`]
types which wrap a simple raw mutex or rwlock type. This has several
benefits: not only does it eliminate a large portion of the work in
implementing custom lock types, it also allows users to write code which is
generic with regards to different lock implementations.

Basic usage of this crate is very straightforward:

- Create a raw lock type. This should only contain the lock state, not any data protected by the lock.
- Implement the `RawMutex`trait for your custom lock type.
- Export your mutex as a type alias for `lock_api::Mutex`, and your mutex guard as a type alias for`lock_api::MutexGuard`. See the[example](https://docs.rs#example)below for details.

This process is similar for [`RwLock`]s, except that two guards need to be
exported instead of one. (Or 3 guards if your type supports upgradable read
locks, see [extension traits](https://docs.rs#extension-traits) below for details)

# Example

```
use ;
use ;
// 1. Define our raw lock type
;
// 2. Implement RawMutex for this type
unsafe
// 3. Export the wrappers. This are the types that your users will actually use.
pub type Spinlock<T> = Mutex;
pub type SpinlockGuard<'a, T> = MutexGuard;
```
# Extension traits

In addition to basic locking & unlocking functionality, you have the option of exposing additional functionality in your lock types by implementing additional traits for it. Examples of extension features include:

- Fair unlocking (`RawMutexFair`,`RawRwLockFair`)
- Lock timeouts (`RawMutexTimed`,`RawRwLockTimed`)
- Downgradable write locks (`RawRwLockDowngradable`)
- Recursive read locks (`RawRwLockRecursive`)
- Upgradable read locks (`RawRwLockUpgrade`)

The `Mutex` and `RwLock` wrappers will automatically expose this additional
functionality if the raw lock type implements these extension traits.

# Cargo features

This crate supports three cargo features:

- `owning_ref`: Allows your lock types to be used with the- `owning_ref`crate.
- `arc_lock`: Enables locking from an- `Arc`. This enables types such as- `ArcMutexGuard`. Note that this requires the- `alloc`crate to be present.

---

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/^1.0

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

---

# crossbeam 0.8.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/crossbeam/^0.8

# Crossbeam

This crate provides a set of tools for concurrent programming:

#### Atomics

- `AtomicCell`
- `AtomicConsume`

#### Data structures

- `deque`
- `ArrayQueue`
- `SegQueue`

#### Memory management

- `epoch`

#### Thread synchronization

- `channel`
- `Parker`
- `ShardedLock`
- `WaitGroup`

#### Utilities

- `Backoff`
- `CachePadded`
- `scope`

*Features marked with (no_std) can be used in  no_std environments.*

*Features marked with (alloc) can be used in*

`no_std` environments, but only if `alloc`
feature is enabled.## Crates

The main `crossbeam` crate just [re-exports](https://docs.rs/src/lib.rs) tools from
smaller subcrates:

- `crossbeam-channel`
- `crossbeam-deque`
- `crossbeam-epoch`
- `crossbeam-queue`
- `crossbeam-utils`

There is one more experimental subcrate that is not yet included in `crossbeam`:

- `crossbeam-skiplist`

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8"
```
## Compatibility

Crossbeam supports stable Rust releases going back at least six months, and every time the minimum supported Rust version is increased, a new minor version is released. Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is 1.61.

## Contributing

Crossbeam welcomes contribution from everyone in the form of suggestions, bug reports, pull requests, and feedback. 💛

If you need ideas for contribution, there are several ways to get started:

- Found a bug or have a feature request?
[Submit an issue](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/issues/new)!
- Issues and PRs labeled with
[feedback wanted](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/issues?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=is%3Aopen+sort%3Aupdated-desc+label%3A%22feedback+wanted%22+)need feedback from users and contributors.
- Issues labeled with
[good first issue](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+sort%3Aupdated-desc+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22)are relatively easy starter issues.

#### RFCs

We also have the [RFCs](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/rfcs) repository for more
high-level discussion, which is the place where we brainstorm ideas and propose
substantial changes to Crossbeam.

You are welcome to participate in any open
[issues](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/rfcs/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+sort%3Aupdated-desc)
or
[pull requests](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/rfcs/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+sort%3Aupdated-desc).

#### Learning resources

If you'd like to learn more about concurrency and non-blocking data structures, there's a
list of learning resources in our [wiki](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/rfcs/wiki),
which includes relevant blog posts, papers, videos, and other similar projects.

Another good place to visit is [merged RFCs](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/rfcs/tree/master/text).
They contain elaborate descriptions and rationale for features we've introduced to
Crossbeam, but keep in mind that some of the written information is now out of date.

#### Conduct

The Crossbeam project adheres to the
[Rust Code of Conduct](https://www.rust-lang.org/policies/code-of-conduct).
This describes the minimum behavior expected from all contributors.

# futures 0.3.32 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures/^0.3

`futures-rs` is a library providing the foundations for asynchronous programming in Rust.
It includes key trait definitions like `Stream`, as well as utilities like `join!`,
`select!`, and various futures combinator methods which enable expressive asynchronous
control flow.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
The current `futures` requires Rust 1.71 or later.

### Feature `std`

Futures-rs works without the standard library, such as in bare metal environments.
However, it has a significantly reduced API surface. To use futures-rs in
a `#[no_std]` environment, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.3",  = false }
```

# tokio 1.52.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tokio/^1

# Tokio

A runtime for writing reliable, asynchronous, and slim applications with the Rust programming language. It is:

-
**Fast**: Tokio's zero-cost abstractions give you bare-metal performance.
-
**Reliable**: Tokio leverages Rust's ownership, type system, and concurrency model to reduce bugs and ensure thread safety.
-
**Scalable**: Tokio has a minimal footprint, and handles backpressure and cancellation naturally.

[Website](https://tokio.rs) |
[Guides](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial) |
[API Docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio) |
[Chat](https://discord.gg/tokio)

## Overview

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- A multithreaded, work-stealing based task [scheduler](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/runtime/index.html).
- A reactor backed by the operating system's event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, etc.).
- Asynchronous [TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/net/index.html)sockets.

These components provide the runtime components necessary for building an asynchronous application.

## Example

A basic TCP echo server with Tokio.

Make sure you enable the full features of the tokio crate on Cargo.toml:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.52.3",  = ["full"] }
```
Then, on your main.rs:

```
use TcpListener;
use ;
async
```
More examples can be found [here](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/tree/master/examples). For a larger "real world" example, see the
[mini-redis](https://github.com/tokio-rs/mini-redis/) repository.

To see a list of the available feature flags that can be enabled, check our
[docs](https://docs.rs/tokio/#feature-flags).

## Getting Help

First, see if the answer to your question can be found in the [Guides](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial) or the
[API documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio). If the answer is not there, there is an active community in
the [Tokio Discord server](https://discord.gg/tokio). We would be happy to try to answer your
question. You can also ask your question on [the discussions page](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/discussions).

## Contributing

:balloon: Thanks for your help improving the project! We are so happy to have
you! We have a [contributing guide](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/docs/contributing/README.md) to help you get involved in the Tokio
project.

## Related Projects

In addition to the crates in this repository, the Tokio project also maintains several other libraries, including:

-
`axum`
-
`hyper`
-
`tonic`
-
`warp`
-
`tower`
-
`tracing``tokio-trace`): A framework for application-level tracing and async-aware diagnostics.
-
`mio``tokio`.
-
`bytes`
-
`loom`

## Changelog

The Tokio repository contains multiple crates. Each crate has its own changelog.

- `tokio`-- [view changelog](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/tokio/CHANGELOG.md)
- `tokio-util`-- [view changelog](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/tokio-util/CHANGELOG.md)
- `tokio-stream`-- [view changelog](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/tokio-stream/CHANGELOG.md)
- `tokio-macros`-- [view changelog](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/tokio-macros/CHANGELOG.md)
- `tokio-test`-- [view changelog](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/tokio-test/CHANGELOG.md)

## Supported Rust Versions

Tokio will keep a rolling MSRV (minimum supported rust version) policy of **at
least** 6 months. When increasing the MSRV, the new Rust version must have been
released at least six months ago. The current MSRV is 1.71.

Note that the MSRV is not increased automatically, and only as part of a minor release. The MSRV history for past minor releases can be found below:

- 1.48 to now - Rust 1.71
- 1.39 to 1.47 - Rust 1.70
- 1.30 to 1.38 - Rust 1.63
- 1.27 to 1.29 - Rust 1.56
- 1.17 to 1.26 - Rust 1.49
- 1.15 to 1.16 - Rust 1.46
- 1.0 to 1.14 - Rust 1.45

Note that although we try to avoid the situation where a dependency transitively increases the MSRV of Tokio, we do not guarantee that this does not happen. However, every minor release will have some set of versions of dependencies that works with the MSRV of that minor release.

## Release schedule

Tokio doesn't follow a fixed release schedule, but we typically make one minor release each month. We make patch releases for bugfixes as necessary.

## Bug patching policy

For the purposes of making patch releases with bugfixes, we have designated certain minor releases as LTS (long term support) releases. Whenever a bug warrants a patch release with a fix for the bug, it will be backported and released as a new patch release for each LTS minor version. Our current LTS releases are:

- `1.47.x`- LTS release until September 2026. (MSRV 1.70)
- `1.51.x`- LTS release until March 2027. (MSRV 1.71)

Each LTS release will continue to receive backported fixes for at least a year. If you wish to use a fixed minor release in your project, we recommend that you use an LTS release.

To use a fixed minor version, you can specify the version with a tilde. For
example, to specify that you wish to use the newest `1.47.x` patch release, you
can use the following dependency specification:

```
tokio = { version = "~1.47", features = [...] }
```
### Previous LTS releases

- `1.8.x`- LTS release until February 2022.
- `1.14.x`- LTS release until June 2022.
- `1.18.x`- LTS release until June 2023.
- `1.20.x`- LTS release until September 2023.
- `1.25.x`- LTS release until March 2024.
- `1.32.x`- LTS release until September 2024.
- `1.36.x`- LTS release until March 2025.
- `1.38.x`- LTS release until July 2025.
- `1.43.x`- LTS release until March 2026.

## License

This project is licensed under the [MIT license](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/master/LICENSE).

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in Tokio by you shall be licensed as MIT, without any additional terms or conditions.

# kanal 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/kanal/0.1.0

# Kanal

**The fast sync and async channel that Rust deserves!**

## What is Kanal

The Kanal library is a Rust implementation of channels inspired by the CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes) model. It aims to help programmers create efficient concurrent programs by providing multi-producer and multi-consumer channels with advanced features for fast communication. The library focuses on unifying message passing between synchronous and asynchronous parts of Rust code, offering a combination of synchronous and asynchronous APIs while maintaining high performance.

## Why Kanal is faster?

- Kanal employs a highly optimized composite technique for the transfer of objects. When the data size is less than or equal to the pointer size, it utilizes serialization, encoding the data as the pointer address. Conversely, when the data size exceeds the pointer size, the protocol employs a strategy similar to that utilized by the Golang programming language, utilizing direct memory access to copy objects from the sender's stack or write directly to the receiver's stack. This composite method not only eliminates unnecessary pointer access but also eliminates heap allocations for bounded(0) channels.
- Kanal utilizes a specially tuned mutex for its channel locking mechanism, made possible by the predictable internal lock time of the channel. That said it's possible to use Rust standard mutex with the `std-mutex`feature and Kanal will perform better than competitors with that feature too.
- Utilizing Rust high-performance compiler and powerful LLVM backend with highly optimized memory access and deeply thought algorithms.

## Usage

To use Kanal in your Rust project, add the following line to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "0.1"
```
Sync channel example:

```
// Initialize a bounded sync channel with a capacity for 8 messages
let  = bounded;
let s = sender.clone;
spawn;
// Receive an example message in another thread
let msg = receiver.recv?;
println!;
// Convert and use channel in async context to communicate between sync and async
spawn;
```
Async channel example:

```
// Initialize a bounded channel with a capacity for 8 messages
let  = bounded_async;
sender.send.await?;
sender.send.await?;
// Clone receiver and convert it to a sync receiver
let receiver_sync = receiver.clone.to_sync;
spawn;
// Spawn a thread and use receiver in sync context
spawn;
```
## Why use Kanal?

- Kanal offers fast and efficient communication capabilities.
- Kanal simplifies communication in and between synchronous and asynchronous contexts, thanks to its flexible API like `as_sync`and`as_async`.
- Kanal provides a clean and intuitive API, making it easier to work with compared to other Rust libraries.
- Similar to Golang, Kanal allows you to close channels using the `Close`function, enabling you to broadcast a close signal from any channel instance and close the channel for both senders and receivers.
- Kanal includes high-performance MPMC (Multiple Producers Multiple Consumers) and SPSC (Single Producer Single Consumer) channels in a single package.

### Benchmark Results

Results are based on how many messages can be passed in each scenario per second.

#### Test types:

- Seq is sequentially writing and reading to a channel in the same thread.
- SPSC is one receiver, and one sender and passing messages between them.
- MPSC is multiple sender threads with only one receiver.
- MPMC is multiple senders and multiple receivers communicating through the same channel.

#### Message types:

- `usize`tests are transferring messages of size hardware pointer.
- `big`tests are transferring messages of 8x the size of the hardware pointer.

N/A means that the test subject is unable to perform the test due to its limitations, Some of the test subjects don't have implementation for size 0 channels, MPMC or unbounded channels.

Machine: `AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-Core Processor`
Rust: `rustc 1.85.1 (4eb161250 2025-03-15)`
Go: `go version go1.24.1 linux/amd64`
OS (`uname -a`): `Linux 6.11.0-19-generic #19~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Mon Feb 17 11:51:52 UTC 2 x86_64`
Date: Jan 25, 2023

#### Why does async outperform sync in some tests?

In certain tests, asynchronous communication may exhibit superior performance compared to synchronous communication. This can be attributed to the context-switching performance of libraries such as tokio, which, similar to Golang, utilize context-switching within the same thread to switch to the next coroutine when a message is ready on a channel. This approach is more efficient than communicating between separate threads. This same principle applies to asynchronous network applications, which generally exhibit better performance compared to synchronous implementations. As the channel size increases, one may observe improved performance in synchronous benchmarks, as the sending threads are able to push data directly to the channel queue without requiring awaiting blocking/suspending signals from receiving threads.
